translations.text: The enemy of truth saw the Lord and Savior, the life-giving God, being proclaimed, and was troubled. He saw the Lord’s coming on a donkey, glorified by us as before, and tried to cause turmoil with the clatter of rattling chariots, to hinder the advance of the donkey. Yet the donkey, walking gently and with a peaceful tread, checked the chariot steeds of the warriors. For he knew that the donkey had been prepared to defeat the chariots and steeds. For the Savior came on a donkey not to show any weakness, but the gentleness of humility, so that he might extinguish arrogance. And because the enemy knew that these things would happen according to the prophetic utterance, he became jealous and raged against the donkey. Yet this was to extinguish the pride of the proud one and bring low the immense arrogance of the one who exalted himself in chariots and steeds.

The blessed prophet rightly announced this beforehand and gave encouragement, saying: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; proclaim and rejoice, daughter of Jerusalem. For behold, your king comes, riding on the foal of a donkey, to destroy the chariots from Ephraim and the steeds from Jerusalem.” Do you see how he softened and brought down swaggering arrogance through gentleness? Just as he removed sufferings through suffering, bound death through death, and exposed the power of the adversary through the wood of the holy cross, so also through the donkey he broke the horse-borne insolence of the one who boasted.

“Rejoice,” says the prophet, “daughter of Zion; exult and proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem.” For it is right and fitting for those who worship God not only to possess the divine gifts themselves, but also to spread the proclamation of his goodness to others. “For behold, your king comes, gentle and humble, seated on a donkey.” He rightly placed “gentle” and “humble” first, to make clear that these were not signs of poverty, but tidings of gentleness and humility. For if someone rides a young donkey because he lacks possessions and has no steeds, this is not counted as goodness and humility, since the constraint of destitution brings him to it. But if someone who has chariots and many steeds sits on a donkey’s foal out of gentleness, he adorns the practice of gentleness with humility. The King of hosts did not lack chariots. The Only-Begotten did not lack chariots and steeds; of him the prophet says, “The chariots of God are ten thousandfold, and thousands are their drivers.” He did not lack chariots, he who harnesses the winds and speeds along with wondrous and unprecedented bridles. Or do you not know that, just as horses serve as mounts for us, [?], according to what David says: “He who rides upon the wings of the winds”?

Now he came on a donkey to overthrow pride through humility and also to proclaim fully, in a figure, the entry of the Gentiles. For the donkey is counted among the unclean animals: Moses set apart as unclean every animal that neither has a divided hoof nor chews the cud. And the donkey, because it neither chews the cud nor has a divided hoof, is counted among the unclean animals. He was fulfilling beforehand the figures of his dispensation that seeks out humanity, for he was going to call the divine, holy people his mount. Just as horses are mounts for a rider, so the souls of the saints are mounts for riders; so also the souls of the saints are mounts for God in their conduct and obedience to his instructive commands. As the prophet says, “You will mount your horses, and your riding brings salvation.” Paul was such an unbroken, unbridled mount, heedless of the divine laws. He grazed in the pastures of the law and kicked against the graces of the gospel. When the Son, the Lord of all, put a bridle on him and mounted him, he said, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad and to kick against the sword.” And since the donkey has bolted and run away from the course of this discourse, let us beseech the Lord of the donkey, who can hold it, lead it, and keep the donkey within the discourse. For he is the one of whom the prophecy says, “He will tie his donkey to the vine.”

Jesus sat on a donkey—he who sits upon the cherubim, who above is awesome because of his divine nature and below is longed for because of his grace and love for humanity. On high the seraphim bow before him with trembling, and on earth he is boldly proclaimed by us who are flesh. For just as his birth above is awesome, so below the freely springing shoot is an object of longing. Jesus sat on a donkey, and the crowds spread their garments before him. The honor was [?], but the honor offered by those honoring him was in no way worthy according to the commandment. For God does not seek gifts from human beings according to his own worthiness, but according to the means of those honoring him. Indeed, there is nothing that could honor God according to his own worthiness. Neither the whole earth nor all heaven joining their voices, nor all the voices of angels and archangels, nor visible and invisible beings becoming tongues, are sufficient to glorify him according to his own worthiness.

He rode on a donkey, he who sits eternally in the heavens. People spread their garments before him, though they ought to have spread out their souls before their garments. You who spread your garments for the donkey to tread upon, spread out your soul as a dwelling for God. This is what John the Baptist also proclaimed: “Prepare the ways of the Lord, and make the [?] paths straight.” This means making souls ready, so that God and the Son of the Lord may enter and dwell in them. Taking palm branches, they went out to meet him. And the one whom the angels glorify in heaven with awe, the children also blessed, rejoicing on earth and saying, “Hosanna!” In the Hebrew language this signifies glorification and great praise.
